paragraphs: But, true to his first position, Rousseau celebrates barbarism as the next best thing to a state of nature; and, addressing the shade of Fabricius, he forgets that the Romans, in conquering the world, never dreamed of setting their own liberty on a firm basis or of extending the reign of virtue. Eager to support his system, he brands every effort of genius as vicious; and, pronouncing the deification of savage virtues, he raises to the rank of demigods men who were scarcely human — the brutal Spartans, who, in defiance of justice and gratitude, slaughtered in cold blood the slaves who had shown themselves to be men by rescuing their oppressors.

Disgusted with artificial manners and virtues, the citizen of Geneva, instead of sifting the subject properly, threw out the wheat with the chaff, without stopping to ask whether the evils from which his ardent soul turned in indignation were the result of civilization or the remnants of barbarism. He saw vice trampling on virtue, and the appearance of goodness taking the place of the reality; he saw talents bent by power to sinister ends, and never thought of tracing this gigantic mischief back to arbitrary power — back to the hereditary distinctions that clash with the mental superiority that naturally raises one man above his fellows. He did not see that royal power, within a few generations, brings idiocy into the noble line, and holds out bait that makes thousands idle and vicious.

Nothing can show the royal character in a more contemptible light than the various crimes that have raised men to the highest rank. Vile intrigues, unnatural crimes and every vice that degrades our nature have been the steps to this exalted eminence; yet millions of men have passively allowed the feeble limbs of the descendants of such rapacious prowlers to rest undisturbed on their bloodstained thrones.

What but a poisonous vapour can hang over society when its chief director has been taught nothing but the invention of crimes, or the stupid routine of childish ceremonies? Will men never be wise? Will they never stop expecting corn from tares, and figs from thistles?

No man, even when the most favourable circumstances combine, can acquire enough knowledge and strength of mind to perform the duties of a king entrusted with unchecked power. How, then, must those duties be violated when his very elevation is an insuperable barrier to gaining either wisdom or virtue — when all his feelings as a man are stifled by flattery, and reflection is shut out by pleasure! Surely it is madness to make the fate of thousands depend on the whim of a weak fellow creature whose very station sinks him NECESSARILY below the lowest of his subjects! But one power should not be thrown down in order to raise up another — for all power intoxicates weak man, and its abuse proves that the more equality is established among men, the more virtue and happiness will reign in society. Yet this, and any similar maxim drawn from simple reason, raises an outcry: the church or the state is in danger if faith in the wisdom of antiquity is not unquestioning; and those who, roused by the sight of human suffering, dare to attack human authority are reviled as despisers of God and enemies of man. These are bitter slanders, yet they reached one of the best of men (Dr. Price), whose ashes still preach peace, and whose memory calls for a respectful pause whenever subjects so close to his heart are discussed.

After attacking the sacred majesty of kings, I shall hardly cause surprise by adding my firm conviction that every profession whose power rests on a strict hierarchy of rank is highly damaging to morality.

A standing army, for example, is incompatible with freedom, because subordination and rigour are the very sinews of military discipline, and despotism is needed to give vigour to enterprises directed by a single will. A spirit inspired by romantic notions of honour — a kind of morality founded on the fashion of the age — can be felt only by a few officers, while the main body must be moved by command, like the waves of the sea; for the strong wind of authority drives the crowd of subordinates forward with headlong fury, though they scarcely know or care why.

Besides, nothing can be so harmful to the morals of the inhabitants of country towns as the occasional residence among them of a set of idle, superficial young men whose only occupation is gallantry, and whose polished manners make vice more dangerous by hiding its ugliness under gay, ornamental drapery. An air of fashion, which is merely a badge of slavery and proves that the soul lacks a strong individual character, overawes simple country people into imitating the vices when they cannot catch the elusive graces of politeness. Every regiment is a chain of despots who, submitting and tyrannizing without exercising their reason, become dead weights of vice and folly on the community. A man of rank or fortune, sure of promotion through influence, has nothing to do but pursue some extravagant whim; while the needy GENTLEMAN, who is to rise, as the saying goes, by his merit, becomes a servile hanger-on or a vile pimp.

Sailors — the naval gentlemen — fit the same description, except that their vices take a different and coarser form. They are more thoroughly idle when they are not carrying out the ceremonial duties of their station, whereas the trivial fluttering of soldiers might be called active idleness. Confined more to the company of men, sailors acquire a taste for broad humour and mischievous pranks; soldiers, who frequently mix with well-bred women, pick up a sentimental cant. But mind is equally out of the question, whether they indulge in the horse-laugh or the polite simper.

May I extend the comparison to a profession in which more mind is certainly to be found? For the clergy have better opportunities for improvement, though subordination cramps their faculties almost as much. The blind submission to forms of belief imposed at university serves as an apprenticeship for the curate who, if he means to rise in his profession, most obsequiously respects the opinion of his rector or patron. Perhaps there can be no more striking contrast than that between the servile, dependent gait of a poor curate and the courtly bearing of a bishop. And the respect and the contempt they inspire make the performance of their separate functions equally useless.

It is very important to observe that every man’s character is, to some degree, formed by his profession. A man of sense may have only a professional cast of features that wears off as you trace his individuality, whereas the weak, common man scarcely ever has any character except what belongs to his corps; at least, all his opinions have been so steeped in the vat consecrated by authority that the faint spirit yielded by the grape of his own vine cannot be distinguished.
Society, therefore, as it becomes more enlightened, should take great care not to establish bodies of men who must necessarily be made foolish or vicious by the very constitution of their profession.

In the infancy of society, when men were just emerging from barbarism, chiefs and priests, pressing on the most powerful springs of savage conduct — hope and fear — must have had unlimited sway. An aristocracy, of course, is naturally the first form of government. But as clashing interests soon lose their balance, a monarchy and a hierarchy break out of the confusion of ambitious struggles, and the foundation of both is secured by feudal tenures. This appears to be the origin of royal and priestly power, and the dawn of civilization. But such combustible materials cannot be kept pent up for long; and as they find an outlet in foreign wars and domestic insurrections, the people acquire some power in the tumult, which obliges their rulers to gloss over their oppression with a show of right. Thus, as wars, agriculture, commerce and literature expand the mind, despots are compelled to make hidden corruption hold on to the power that was formerly seized by open force.* And this deadly, lurking gangrene is spread most quickly by luxury and superstition, the sure dregs of ambition. The idle puppet of a court first becomes a luxurious monster or a fastidious sensualist, and then makes the contagion that his unnatural state spreads into the instrument of tyranny.

(*Footnote. Men of ability scatter seeds that grow up and have a great influence on the formation of opinion; and once public opinion gains the upper hand, through the exercise of reason, the overthrow of arbitrary power is not far off.)

It is the pestilential purple of royalty that turns the progress of civilization into a curse and warps the understanding, until men of sensibility doubt whether the expansion of the intellect produces a greater share of happiness or of misery. But the nature of the poison points to the antidote; and had Rousseau climbed one step higher in his investigation, or could his eye have pierced the foggy atmosphere that he almost disdained to breathe, his active mind would have darted forward to contemplate the perfection of man in the establishment of true civilization, instead of taking his ferocious flight back to the night of sensual ignorance.
